# Research Design

Apart from a general, descriptive analysis of the data, my approach to the research question can be divided into four different perspectives concerning (1) the role of Greenlandic-Faroese cooperation in the Northatlantic Party Group until 2011, (2) bloc cohesion and party alignment, (3) measurable power in roll call votes, and (4) voting in Folketinget roll call votes as way of exercising cross-parliamentary control.

## Theoretical Approach

<!-- * Hypothesis: causal relationship between two variables: the more, the less...
* Hypothesis in its own paragraph and in italics -->

A review of existing literature showed that the Northatlantic MPs' work in Folketinget has only recently started to attract scientific attention, and until now, voting behavior has not been a factor at all. The first step, therefore, is a descriptive analysis of the available data, including relevant MPs and scraped voting records. Generally, Northatlantic MPs are expected not to take part in parliamentary voting, even though "they are perceived to be more and more involved" [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 7, translation MT].

<!-- section 1 Participation pre/post 2011 -->
Looking at party group memberships, Bille observes shifts in MPs' behavior over the years [-@billeFaeroskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025]. Overall, @harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022 [19] detects a higher level of activity for Greenlandic MPs when compared to Faroese MPs. Her analysis uses committee memberships and parliamentary questioning as variables, as well as longer absences. Higher levels of activity from the Greenlandic side is also a finding of @harderCaseInnovativeParliamentary2022, analysing questioning as a tool for cross-parliamentary control. Based on these assessments, I also assume Greenlandic MPs to be more active in roll call voting than the Faroese members. Drawing on prevailing views of the Northatlantic MPs' role in parliament, the overall level of voting activity is still expected be quite low.

From 2001 until the 2011 election, three MPs from Greenland and the Faroe Islands cooperated in their own parliamentary group [*Den Nordatlantiske Gruppe*, @harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 18]. @harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025 [11-12] hypothesises a relation between the existence of party competition -- after the Northatlantic Group had been dissolved in 2011 -- and an increase in parliamentary activity, more precisely in questioning related to cross-parliamentary control. I take this hypothesis and apply it to participation in roll call voting as well, expecting a relative increase in participation after the 2011 election:

* H~1~: *Participation in roll call voting increases after the Northatlantic Group is dissolved after the 2011 general election.*

<!-- section 2: Bloc Cohesion vs. Party Alignment -->
The second perspective concerns the voting records themselves and whether Northatlantic MPs vote as one bloc. @harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022 [18] finds that MPs support coalitions that belong to the same political bloc as their own party, aligning with findings about high levels of party cohesion in Folketinget [@ejnarhansenReconsideringPartyDistances2008, 266]. The relevant political parties (see [Appendix](#list-of-parties)) can be classified as belonging to either the left/red or right/blue bloc of Danish politics. At the same time, the more important cleavage for political parties in Greenland and the Faroe Islands is between separatism and unionism [@ackrenExploringRoleRegional2019, 27]. And since Greenlandic, Faroese and Danish party systems are separate entities, additional "judgments need to be made as to what parliamentary coalitions the four North Atlantic seats would likely caucus or collaborate with" [@kurrild-klitgaardElectionInversionsCoalitions2013, 130]. I therefore expect to find patterns showing that voting cohesion among Northatlantic MPs based on their origin is more prevalent than cohesion with the Danish political bloc they would be assigned to based on their party membership.

* H~2~: *Voting cohesion among MPs from the same constituency is higher than voting cohesion among MPs from the same political bloc.*

There are examples of MPs supporting the other political bloc such as when Aleqa Hammond, at the time member of social democratic Siumut, agreed to support the right-wing coalition of Venstre, Liberal Alliance and Det Konservative Folkeparti [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 17; @uldumKommentatorUdpegelseAf2016]. Faroese unionist MP Anna Falkenberg, on the other hand, stated that she considers herself to be part of Venstre's Folketinget group and, thus, the Danish (!) government [@falkenbergFaeroskPolitikerTil2025]. And during election campaigns some of the Northatlantic candidates refuse to commit to joining one of the blocs, even though the political profile of their party clearly points in one direction [cf. @engelundMorgenpostFraGronland2026a; @joensenNordatlantiskePartierVil2022].

<!-- section 3: Pivotality -->
Thirdly, individual voting behavior is rarely a decisive factor -- since party cohesion in Folketinget is generally high [@ejnarhansenReconsideringPartyDistances2008, 266; @hansenRealBorgenDanish2020, 3] and, after policy has been negotiated in committees, the result of the plenary vote is usually known in advance [@hansenRealBorgenDanish2020; @arterNordicParliamentsMuchofamuchness2016, 214]. But, as noted above, party lines appear to be a less important factor for Northatlantic MPs and they make use of voting power when it is presented to them also across blocs [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 18; @skjaevelandModellingGovernmentFormation2009, 723]. Numerous examples exist for such situations: The 2022 Folketinget election resulted in a left/red majority of 90 MPs due to three left-wing Northatlantic politicians [@frostLokkeRaserNordatlantiske2022]. After the 2015 and 2007 elections, Northatlantic votes helped to keep the narrow majority of the conservative bloc, and in the 2011--2015 parliament, three Northatlantic MPs brought the left/red bloc up to 92 votes. After the 2007 election, the right/blue bloc relied on a Faroese MP to secure a parliamentary majority [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 19; @mollerForskerNordatlantiskeMandater2026]. The result of the elections in 1998, 1971, 1960 and 1957 led to similar situations [@skjaevelandModellingGovernmentFormation2009, 723; @skjaevelandGovernmentFormationDenmark2003, 448; @millerFriendsRivals1996, 71]. In some isolated votes, the Northatlantic votes have become relevant even though there was a clear parliamentary basis from Danish parties alone: A vote of no confidence against a member of cabinet was blocked in 2025 by a "Northatlantic safety buoy" [@danielsenTeorienKanJeg2025, translation MT]. In 2008, the pressure resulting from the mere possibility of using Northatlantic votes in a proposal on immigration policy lead to a change in another party's stance [@cleggParliamentaryRepresentationOverseas2022, 239; @gadGronlandskeFolketingsmedlemmer2022] -- illustrating how, for Greenlandic and Faroese MPs, the question of voting behavior can be connected with a lot of publicity. This leads to the third hypothesis about a connection of pivotality and participation:

* H~3~: *The closer the parliamentary balance between government and opposition, the more often Northatlantic MPs participate in roll call votes.*

While numerical closeness captures the potential of pivotality at the level of individual votes, I assume the structure of the coalition government to be a factor in participation rates as well. During the timeframe covered by the dataset, the work of parliament has largely been based on the red/blue-dichotomy of political blocs [@green-pedersenBlokpolitikOgNye2020, 312; @skjaevelandUnderstandingPoliticalUnderstanding2020, 115] -- the exception being the Frederiksen II cabinet (2022--2026) consisting of Socialdemokratiet, Moderaterne and Venstre, a government with parties from both blocs but still without a numerical majority on their own. Even though Northatlantic MPs usually are considered to belong to one of the two Danish party blocs and they tend to support the bloc their own party belongs to [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 18], I expect participation rates to go up in cross-bloc minority governments compared to times of bloc politics: The cabinet parties still rely on support from other parties, which for those parties would mean working across blocs. Based on the examples of crossing party and bloc lines mentioned previously, I assume the Northatlantic MPs to be less reluctant support cabinets featuring parties of the opposite bloc in comparison to 'domestic' Danish parties. However, since there is only one example of this form of cross-bloc minority government in the dataset, I only include this as an addition to the main part of H~3~ which is based on parliamentary balance regardless of its direction.

<!-- section 4: Cross-Parliamentary Control -->
Last but not least, I turn to the question of cross-parliamentary control. From this perspective, Northatlantic MPs use their mandates in the Danish parliament to engage in activities with the aim to control the goverment in Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands. Folketinget appears to be a suitable case to study this concept -- not only because the "particularly strong" [@helboepedersenParliamentFOLKETINGETPowerful2020, 102] instruments available to MPs to control Folketinget itself, but also because of its status as second-order parliament from a Northatlantic perspective [@harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025, 3]. Usually, parliamentary oversight is considered to manifest itself through questioning activity [@westPoliticalPartiesParliamentary2025, 969]. Harder, looking at Greenlandic MPs' questions in Folketinget, finds that there is no significant connection between the number of questions posed and whether the MP is affiliated with the Danish <!-- fixme??? ---> government or oppoisition [-@harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025, 17]. However, she hypothesises that MPs "will especially engage in cross-parliamentary control when they belong to parties that are in opposition within the government system where they seek to control the government" [@harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025, 12]. Within the context of this paper, this is transferred to roll call voting as well:

* H~4~: *Northatlantic MPs participate in more roll call votes when their party is in opposition in their home parliament.*

The underlying assumption then is that the participation in roll call votes in Folketinget can -- in the context of the Northatlantic representation -- also be seen as a form of cross-parliamentary control. In this sense, casting votes is expected to work as control mechanism in so far as it comes with increased publicity as demonstrated above, and has an impact similar to posing parliamentary questions: promoting political debate in parliament as well as agenda setting in media coverage, acting "as party agents to support their colleagues at home" [@harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025, 7].

## Empirical Strategy

I am using the [*nordatlantisk-ft*](https://mtwente.github.io/nordatlantisk-ft) dataset which contains voting records of Folketinget members from Greenland and the Faroe Islands. Since Folketinget does not provide ready-to-use open datasets but metadata only [@berntzenParliamentaryOpenData2019, 9], I had to create both workflow and dataset myself. The dataset is the result of a pipeline in R, taking a list of MPs as input and then scraping voting records and metadata from Folketinget's Open Data Platform [@folketingetFolketingetsAbneData2026]. Both workflow and dataset are version-controlled using a git-based template including long-term archival on Zenodo [@mahrOneTemplateRule2025a], and are accompanied by extensive metadata and documentation to ensure reproducibility. [Codebook](https://mtwente.github.io/nordatlantisk-ft/docs/codebook.html) and [source code](https://github.com/mtwente/nordatlantisk-ft) are available via GitHub. 

For my analysis, I am going to use the data available as of `r format(file.info(here("data", "processed", "northatlantic_ft.rds"))$mtime, "%B %d, %Y")` [@twenteNordatlantiskft2026]. At this point, *nordatlantisk-ft* comprises `r length(unique(northatlantic_ft$vote_id))` records of votes by Northatlantic MPs between `r format(min(northatlantic_ft$date), "%B %d, %Y")` and `r format(max(northatlantic_ft$date), "%B %d, %Y")`[^valg26]. The dataset contains metadata on each record -- e.g. date and topic of each vote or the overall roll call result, covering votes on `r length(unique(northatlantic_ft$roll_call_id))` proposals in Folketinget. Additionally, there is information on cabinets, election results and party changes over time. This paper also includes a general description of the data as starting point for investigating the parliamentary work of the Northatlantic MPs.

[^valg26]: PM Mette Frederiksen announced the date for the next general election to Folketinget (`r format(as.Date("2026-03-24"), "%B %d, %Y")`) on `r format(as.Date("2026-02-26"), "%B %d, %Y")`. The data used for this analysis thus does not contain records on voting behavior during the election campaign (if there are any).

<!-- - case selection/overview data (temporal and spatial), unit of analysis
- measurement dependent variable (and data source)
- measurement independent and control variables (and data source)
- methodological approach (why this one?) -->

#### H~1~: Participation Before/After 2009

* fixme overall: * unit of observation? unit of analysis?

```{r h1-analysis-setup}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

## define end date of Parliamentary Group (start was before dataset inception)
northatlantic_ft <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  mutate(
    postgroup2009 = ifelse(date >= as.Date("2009-08-14"), 1, 0),
    postgroup2011 = ifelse(date >= as.Date("2011-09-15"), 1, 0)
  )

northatlantic_ft <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  mutate(
    treated = ifelse(origin == "GL", 1, 0)
  )

# interaction variable between postgroup20* and treatment
northatlantic_ft <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  mutate(
    did2009 = postgroup2009 * treated,
    did2011 = postgroup2011 * treated
  )

# estimate DID models
didreg2009 <- lm(participation ~ treated + postgroup2009 + did2009, data = northatlantic_ft)
didreg2011 <- lm(participation ~ treated + postgroup2011 + did2011, data = northatlantic_ft)
```

A difference-in-differences approach [@callawayDifferenceinDifferencesMultipleTime2021] is used to find out if ending formal cooperation in the Northatlantic Group had any effect on the share of participation in roll call votes. Only the Greenlandic MPs can be included for testing the hypothesis: In this setting, party competition is only realised outside of the Northatlantic Group's cooperation. And since only one of the Faroese MPs ever joined the Northatlantic Group, there should be no change in the level of party competition to be detected within the Faroese delegation. However, this enables me to use the Faroese MPs as a control group and compare the results between Greenlandic MPs -- who worked together within the Northatlantic Group -- and the Faroese MPs (who did not). Because Greenland and the Faroe Islands have different party systems [@kurrild-klitgaardElectionInversionsCoalitions2013, 129--130], I assume no party competition to be present across the two constituencies.

The parliamentary group existed from 2001 to 2011. However, during its last two years, it only had two members -- Juliane Henningsen (IA/GL) and Høgni Hoydal (E/FO), after the second Greenlandic MP, Lars-Emil Johansen (SIU/GL), left in 2009 [@harderSupplerendeMaterialeFaeroske2022, 13][^exact]. In line with the hypothesis by @harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025 [11-12], the group-based incentive for increased party competition should come in effect already at that point, since the two remaining MPs in the parliamentary group -- one Greenlandic, one Faroese -- would not engage in party-based competition anyway. If the end of formal parliamentary cooperation lead to a change in voting behavior for the two Greenlandic MPs, it should therefore be already visible in 2009, before the actual end of the Northatlantic Group in 2011.

[^exact]: For the analysis, the exact date of the group change is assumed to be `r format(as.Date("2009-08-14"), "%B %d, %Y")` based on reporting by @sermitsiaq.agLarsEmilForladerNordatlantiske2009.

Each MP is regarded as participating in a roll call if there is a vote either for, against, or neither for nor against recorded in the corresponding observation in the dataset. To find out the differences between participation rates, the dataset is split into two groups -- MPs from Greenland and MPs from the Faroe Islands. I then split the data again based on a dummy variable using 2009 as the cut-off date. For comparison, I run the same test again using the official ending date of the parliamentary group (2011). I then estimate a linear model with the difference in difference coefficient. For this model, I use `participation` as dependent variable with binary values indicating whether an MP participated in a roll call vote. The key independent variable is an interaction term between a treatment indicator for Greenlandic MPs (`treated`) and a post-group period dummy (`postgroup2009`/`postgroup2011`). This interaction captures the difference-in-differences estimate of the effect of increased party competition on participation behavior.

#### H~2~: Bloc Cohesion

```{r prepare-h2-analysis}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

## define bloc affiliations
### defined in _setupR.R include

## filter/subset original dataset
northatlantic_ft_present_only <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  filter(participation == TRUE)

## add GL/FO party blocs
northatlantic_ft_present_only <- northatlantic_ft_present_only %>%
  mutate(
    party_bloc = case_when(
      party %in% left_parties   ~ "left",
      party %in% center_parties ~ "center",
      party %in% right_parties  ~ "right",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    )
  ) %>%
  relocate(party_bloc, .after = party)

## pivot wider
northatlantic_ft_participation_wide <- northatlantic_ft_present_only %>%
  select(roll_call_id, party, vote_type_id) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = party, values_from = vote_type_id)
```

To assess voting cohesion among North Atlantic MPs, I employ two complementary methods: Pairwise agreement rates and Krippendorff's Alpha as an additional measure. Using roll call votes as unit of analysis, agreement between two MPs is defined as both of them having the same value of the variable `vote_type_id` for the same roll call vote, e.g. both voting `for` one proposal. One vote (or more) `for` and one vote (or more) `against` is no agreement, meaning disagreement, or no cohesive voting behavior. First, I remove all observations where none of the four MPs actually cast a vote. This leaves `r length(unique(northatlantic_ft_present_only$roll_call_id))` roll calls with at least one recorded vote (`r scales::percent(length(unique(northatlantic_ft_present_only$roll_call_id))/length(unique(northatlantic_ft$roll_call_id)), accuracy = 0.1)` of all observations) for further processing.

```{r krippendorffs-alpha-setup}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

vote_matrix <- northatlantic_ft_participation_wide %>%
  select(-roll_call_id) %>%
  as.matrix()

# transpose: parties = rows, roll calls = columns
vote_matrix_t <- t(vote_matrix)
```

I then calculate Krippendorff's Alpha for the dataset of non-absent records as a summary measure of overall agreement. Krippendorff's Alpha appears to be a reasonable choice for measuring agreement with the dataset at hand: It is conceptualised to be applicable to small data sets with any number of observers, handling missing values and correcting for agreement that is to be expected by chance [@krippendorffContentAnalysisIntroduction2004, 222]. The resulting $\alpha$  represents the "proportion of the observed to expected above-chance agreement" [@krippendorffContentAnalysisIntroduction2004, 229], with $1 \geq \alpha \geq 0$ as possible values. $\alpha = 1$ then indicates perfect agreement between observers (MPs), and $\alpha = 0$ means that all observed agreements can be explained as matters of chance, ie. the absence of actual agreement between MPs.<!--Negative values for $\alpha$ would indicate a state of systematic disagreement.-->

After determining how much co-voting behavior there is in my dataset using Krippendorff's Alpha, I then calculate pairwise agreement rates myself to investigate possible ways to explain the observed agreement. Pairwise agreement rates are considered in three different comparative settings: Based on MP origin (Are the agreeing/disagreeing MPs from the same constituency?), affiliation with one of the political blocs (Do the agreeing/disagreeing MPs belong to the same bloc?) and their party's stance on independence (Do the parties of the agreeing/disagreeing MPs share the same view on their territory's independence from Denmark?).

```{r pairwise-agreement-setup}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

pairwise_agreement <- function(votes) {
  votes <- na.omit(votes)
  if (length(votes) < 2) return(NA)
  
  pairs <- combn(votes, 2)
  mean(pairs[1, ] == pairs[2, ])
}

cohesion_df <- northatlantic_ft_participation_wide %>%
  rowwise() %>%
  mutate(cohesion = pairwise_agreement(c_across(-roll_call_id))) %>%
  ungroup()
```

To do so, I create a subset of MPs’ votes, again only including roll calls with non-absent records. For each observed roll call vote, I take the registered votes and compare all possible combinations to check whether the two MPs cast the same type of vote. Looking only at cases where at least two MPs cast a vote so there can actually be (dis)agreement, the number of observations is further reduced to `r sum(complete.cases(cohesion_df$cohesion))` (`r scales::percent(sum(complete.cases(cohesion_df$cohesion))/nrow(cohesion_df), accuracy = 0.1)` of roll call votes with non-absent records or `r scales::percent(sum(complete.cases(cohesion_df$cohesion))/length(unique((northatlantic_ft$roll_call_id))), accuracy = 0.01)` of all recorded roll call votes). 

```{r pairwise-agreement-origin}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

pairs_df <- northatlantic_ft_present_only %>%
  select(roll_call_id, party, origin, vote_type_id, party_bloc, gvt_bloc_dk) %>%
  mutate(party = as.character(party)) %>%
  inner_join(., ., by = "roll_call_id", suffix = c("_1", "_2"), relationship = "many-to-many") %>%
  filter(party_1 < party_2) %>%  # avoid duplicates and self-pairs
  mutate(
    agree = vote_type_id_1 == vote_type_id_2,
    same_origin = origin_1 == origin_2
  )

 ### reformat gvt_bloc_dk as control variable
pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(party_bloc_dk_gvt = gvt_bloc_dk_1) %>%
  relocate(party_bloc_dk_gvt, .before = agree) %>%
  select(-gvt_bloc_dk_1, -gvt_bloc_dk_2)

origin_agreement_rate <- pairs_df %>%
  group_by(same_origin) %>%
  summarise(
    agreement_rate = round(mean(agree, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3),
    n = n()
  )
```

```{r pairwise-agreement-bloc}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Compare left/right bloc agreement
pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(
    same_bloc = case_when(
      party_1 %in% left_parties & party_2 %in% left_parties ~ TRUE,
      party_1 %in% right_parties & party_2 %in% right_parties ~ TRUE,
      party_1 %in% center_parties & party_2 %in% center_parties ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )

bloc_agreement_rate <- pairs_df %>%
  group_by(same_bloc) %>%
  summarise(
    agreement_rate = round(mean(agree, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3),
    n = n()
  )
```

```{r pairwise-agreement-independence}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Compare independence/non-independence blocs
pairs_df <- pairs_df %>%
  mutate(
    same_independence_stance = case_when(
      party_1 %in% pro_independence_parties & party_2 %in% pro_independence_parties ~ TRUE,
      party_1 %in% against_independence_parties & party_2 %in% against_independence_parties ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )

independence_agreement_rate <- pairs_df %>%
  group_by(same_independence_stance) %>%
  summarise(
    agreement_rate = round(mean(agree, na.rm = TRUE), digits = 3),
    n = n()
  )

## same_independence_stance = TRUE => cohesion across parties with the same stance on independence
## same_independence_stance = FALSE => cohesion across parties with different stances on independence
```

Three more boolean variables are added to record whether the two MPs in question (1) share the same constituency, (2) are affiliated with the same political bloc, and whether (3) their parties hold the same position on their territory's independence from Denmark (cf. Appendix, @tbl-blocs).

#### H~3~: Pivotality

```{r pivotality-setup}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# calculate margin of votes
northatlantic_ft$margin <- abs(northatlantic_ft$ft_for - northatlantic_ft$ft_against)

# blokpolitik as variable
northatlantic_ft <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  mutate(
    cross_bloc_gvt = ifelse(gvt_bloc_dk == "across", 1, 0)
  )
```

```{r pivotality-models}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Model 1a: Closeness/Participation
rq3_closevote <- glm(
  participation ~ close_vote,
  data = northatlantic_ft,
  family = binomial
)

# Model 1b: Closeness/Participation plus Cabinet Type
rq3_closevote_gvt_dk <- glm(
  participation ~ close_vote + cross_bloc_gvt,
  data = northatlantic_ft,
  family = binomial
)

# Model 2a: Cabinet Party Seats/Participation
rq3_cabinet_seats <- glm(
  participation ~ cabinet_parties_seats,
  data = northatlantic_ft,
  family = binomial
)

# Model 2b: Cabinet Party Seats/Participation plus Cabinet Type
rq3_cabinet_seats_with_bloc <- glm(
  participation ~ cabinet_parties_seats + cross_bloc_gvt,
  data = northatlantic_ft,
  family = binomial
)

all_models_rq3 <- list("Model 1a" = rq3_closevote,
                       "Model 1b" = rq3_closevote_gvt_dk,
                       "Model 2a" = rq3_cabinet_seats,
                       "Model 2b" = rq3_cabinet_seats_with_bloc)

models_1ab_rq3 <- list("Model 1a" = rq3_closevote,
                       "Model 1b" = rq3_closevote_gvt_dk)

models_2ab_rq3 <- list("Model 2a" = rq3_cabinet_seats,
                       "Model 2b" = rq3_cabinet_seats_with_bloc)
```

<!-- * H~3~: *The closer the parliamentary balance between government and opposition, the more often Northatlantic MPs participate in roll call votes.* -->

The question whether Northatlantic MPs take part in more roll call votes the closer the number of seats for government and opposition blocs are together is addressed in different ways with individual votes as unit of analysis. Again using the boolean `participation` as dependent variable, I try explaining the outcome using two main models.

In a first step, I identify roll call votes with a close result, defined as a voting result where the difference between votes in favor and votes against a proposal is less or equal than four votes. In these cases, the four Northatlantic MPs would theoretically be able to flip the result themselves. This is the case for `r scales::percent(sum(northatlantic_ft$close_vote, na.rm = TRUE)/sum(!northatlantic_ft$close_vote, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.01)` of the observations in the dataset. I then estimate a generalized linear model with `participation` (`TRUE`/`FALSE`) as dependent variable and `close_vote` as independent variable (`TRUE`/`FALSE`).

In this approach, I use the outcome of the vote as variable to predict the participation of the Northatlantic MPs. Of course, the margin of the voting result is only known after the vote has already taken place and can not be a decisive factor in a prediction. But, as mentioned above, the overall outcome of a vote is usually known in advance so it is fair to assume MPs can anticipate close results to some extent. I therefore deemed it justified to use this setup -- not with the actual result margins as numerical variable, but instead with a working definition of closeness as a binary variable -- at least for comparison with other models.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-cabinet-seats
#| fig-height: 3
#| fig-cap: Number of seats in parliament held by cabinet parties, with a majority requiring $\\\geq$ 90 seats. Dashed lines indicate election dates.

# filter 2001 election
elections_lines <- elections_ft %>%
  filter(date > as.Date("2001-11-20"))

cabinet_seats <- ggplot(northatlantic_ft, aes(x = date, y = cabinet_parties_seats)) +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Folketing elections
  geom_vline(
    data = elections_lines,
    aes(xintercept = as.Date(date), linetype = election_type),
    color = "#000000",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Folketing Election" = "longdash"),
    name = ""
  ) +
  
  geom_hline(yintercept = 90, color = "#000000", linewidth = 0.3) +
  
  theme_nordatlantisk_basis() +
    theme(
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y.left = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#777777", linewidth = 0.05),
    legend.position = "none"
  )

cabinet_seats
```

The second main model instead uses the number of seats in parliament held by cabinet parties as independent variable for trying to predict the Northatlantic MPs' voting behavior. For each observation in the dataset, I calculated the number of seats based on the election results between 2001 and 2026 [@danmarksstatistikFolketingsvalget31Oktober2024; @danmarksstatistikValgteKandidaterOg2026]. Only cabinet parties are included in this number, support parties (neither *støttepartier* nor *parlamentarisk grundlag*) are not counted.

Since MPs can change party memberships during their time in parliament, I tracked those changes as well and incorporated them into the data to achieve a fine-grained representation of the composition of Folketinget at any given date (@fig-cabinet-seats). While MPs switching parties rarely change the overall allocation of power between the political blocs, it is known to influence decisions from time to time [@nielsenPartiskiftFolketinget195320152017, 62], and these situations being the starting point for this whole paper, I decided to map the seat distribution for each date individually on party level.

Information on MP party affiliation does not seem to be available in machine-readable format on Folketinget's Open Data Platform, which is why I relied on the pre-existing records courtesy of @folkevalgte.dkPartiskift2026. I found minor inconsistencies between [folkevalgte.dk](https://folkevalgte.dk) and other possible data sources such as Folketinget's free text MP biographies or the relatively comprehensive record keeping on Wikipedia. But this only appears to concern smaller and/or short-lived parties such as Fremad [cf. @mollerAmmitzbollOgEgelund2020]. I therefore decided to go with the data from folkevalgte.dk to have a single source of data where record keeping appears to be consistent over the years. Seat distribution after elections and the subsequent party shifts are processed[^rds] using R and merged with the main voting records dataset. I can then estimate the second generalised linear model, this time using `cabinet_parties_seats` as independent variable.

[^rds]: This dataset is [available](https://github.com/mtwente/counting-to-90/tree/main/data/processed) alongside the other data used for this project.

In line with my argument that Northatlantic MPs can be expected to be more inclined to support cross-bloc minority cabinets due to their local political parties being less firmly affiliated with Danish political blocs, I add another dependent variable to open up a second perspective on the role of pivotality in participation rates. The alternative version of both models additionally includes `cross_bloc_gvt` -- again a binary variable which is `TRUE` for observations during cabinets formed by parties from either the left or right bloc, but `FALSE` for observations during cabinets including parties across blocs (although, as mentioned above, this only translates to one cabinet at the time). This allows me to assess whether participation by Northatlantic MPs is shaped not only by the numerical balance of power, but also by the broader configuration of political competition.

#### H~4~: Cross-Parliamentary Control

<!-- H4: Northatlantic MPs participate in more roll call votes when their party is in opposition in their home parliament -->

```{r rq4-setup}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

northatlantic_ft <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  mutate(
    opposition_home = ifelse(gvt_party_at_home == TRUE, 0, 1)
  )

# descriptive comparison
rq4_table <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  group_by(opposition_home) %>%
  summarise(
    participation_rate = mean(participation),
    n = n()
  )

chisq <- chisq.test(
  table(northatlantic_ft$participation, northatlantic_ft$opposition_home)
)
```

For the question whether there is a relation between the MPs' participation in roll call votes in Folketinget and whether their party is part of the government in Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands, I recoded the existing binary `gvt_party_at_home` variable as `opposition_home` to make it easier to interpret the results with the way the hypothesis is framed. `opposition_home` is used as independent variable for this hypothesis, with `participation` again being the dependent variable.

A first look at the data shows that MPs of parties in opposition in the Greenlandic resp. Faroese political systems participate in `r scales::percent(rq4_table$participation_rate[2], accuracy = 0.01)` of roll call votes in Folketinget, while MPs whose party is part of the cabinet at the time of observation have a participation rate of `r scales::percent(rq4_table$participation_rate[1], accuracy = 0.01)`. A $\chi^2$ test indicates a significant difference between the observed participation rate and the level of participation expected if there were no relation between the variables (p < 0.001).

For the analysis, I estimate a generalised linear model as a baseline with the dependent and independent variable specified above. In a second model, I include the number of seats held in parliament by Danish cabinet parties as a control variable, as the analysis concerning H~3~ suggested this might be of relevance.

```{r crosscontrol-models}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# logistic regression
rq4_model <- glm(
  participation ~ opposition_home,
  data = northatlantic_ft,
  family = binomial
)

rq4_model_control <- glm(
  participation ~ opposition_home + cabinet_parties_seats,
  data = northatlantic_ft,
  family = binomial
)

all_models_rq4 <- list("Baseline" = rq4_model,
                       #"Origin-Based" = rq4_interaction,
                       "Control Model" = rq4_model_control)
```

# Dataset Description

## MPs {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Since 1953, two MPs are elected in both Greenland and the Faroe Islands to join the 175 MPs from Denmark proper in Folketinget. Before the 1953 reform, Greenland did not have any parliamentary representation in Folketinget, as opposed to the Faroe Islands with one guaranteed seat since 1849 [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 8-9; @kjaerDanskeFolketingsmedlemmerParlamentarisk2004]. According to @harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022 [7], it is usually experienced politicians that are elected to represent the Faroe Islands constituency[^study], even though the job apparently has low priority compared to holding office 'at home' [@ackrenExploringRoleRegional2019, 22; cf. @harderCrossparliamentaryControl2025, 8; @johannesenUniHolmJohannesen2016].

[^study]: No comparable study exists for MPs from Greenland apart from the short MP profiles available in Danmarks Nationalleksikon [@billeFaeroskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025; @billeGronlandskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025].

In the time frame covered by Folketinget's Open Data Platform, there have been `r nrow(mp_names)` individual politicians from Greenland or the Faroe Islands who served as MPs (@tbl-MPs). `r sum(mp_names$origin == "GL")` of them are members of Greenlandic parties, and `r sum(mp_names$origin == "FO")` are representing Faroese parties. For MPs representing Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands in election periods earlier than `r format(min(northatlantic_ft$date), "%B %Y")`, see the list assembled by @harderSupplerendeMaterialeFaeroske2022.

`r sum(mp_names$substitute == TRUE)` of the politicians that are part of this dataset joined Folketinget in the role of a substitute member[^subst], filling in for one of the `r sum(mp_names$substitute == FALSE)` originally elected MPs while they were on leave [cf. @harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 12-13]. @fig-mandates shows membership periods and substitute members on a timeline for the duration that is covered by this dataset. Earlier membership periods of Edmund Joensen, Lisbeth Petersen, Høgni Hoydal and Tórbjørn Jacobsen are cut off from the timeline since there are no voting records available online earlier than `r format(min(northatlantic_ft$date), "%B %d, %Y")`.

[^subst]: Doris Jakobsen (SIU), Lisbeth Petersen (B), Magni Arge (E) and Sjúrður Skaale (C) all first became MPs as substitute members, but later joined as regular MPs after a general election.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-mandates
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-cap: Timeline of MPs from Greenland and the Faroe Islands during the timeframe covered by this dataset. Substitutions shorter than three weeks are plotted as dots for better visibility.

# remove pre-2000 MPs (Edmund Joensen's and Lisbeth Petersen's first terms)
MP_dates <- MP_dates %>%
  filter(end >= as.Date("2000-01-01")) %>%
  mutate(origin = factor(origin, levels = c("GL", "FO")))

# Order MPs by first start date for nicer plotting
MP_dates <- MP_dates %>%
  group_by(origin, plotting_name) %>%
  mutate(first_start = min(start)) %>%
  ungroup()

# build facet-specific ordering
levels_gl <- MP_dates %>%
  filter(origin == "GL") %>%
  distinct(plotting_name, first_start) %>%
  arrange(desc(first_start)) %>%
  pull(plotting_name)

levels_fo <- MP_dates %>%
  filter(origin == "FO") %>%
  distinct(plotting_name, first_start) %>%
  arrange(desc(first_start)) %>%
  pull(plotting_name)

MP_dates <- MP_dates %>%
  mutate(
    plotting_name = case_when(
      origin == "GL" ~ factor(plotting_name, levels = levels_gl),
      origin == "FO" ~ factor(plotting_name, levels = levels_fo)
    )
  )

ggplot(MP_dates, aes(x = start,
                     xend = end,
                     y = plotting_name,
                     yend = plotting_name,
                     color = substitute)) +

  # for correct order of MPs across facets and scales
  geom_blank(aes(y = plotting_name)) +

  # Segments for all regular MPs and long-term substitutions
  geom_segment(
    data = MP_dates %>%
      filter(
        substitute == FALSE |
          (substitute == TRUE & !is.na(end) & as.numeric(end - start) >= 21)
      ),
    linewidth = 4,
    lineend = "butt"
  ) +

  # Points for short-term substitutions
geom_point(
  data = MP_dates %>%
    filter(
      substitute == TRUE &
        !is.na(end) &
        as.numeric(end - start) < 21
    ),
  aes(
    x = start,
    fill = substitute
  ),
  shape = 21,
  size = 1.5,
  stroke = 0.2,
  color = "#777777"
  ) +

  scale_color_manual(
    values = c("FALSE" = "#6195CF", "TRUE" = "#F7CB45"),
    labels = c("Regular", "Substitute")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
  values = c("FALSE" = "#6195CF", "TRUE" = "#F7CB45"),
  guide = "none"
  ) +
  
  labs(color = "Membership") +

  # Folketing elections
  geom_vline(
    data = elections_ft,
    aes(xintercept = as.Date(date), linetype = election_type),
    color = "#000000",
    linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = c("Folketing Election" = "longdash"),
    name = ""
  ) +

  facet_grid(
    origin ~ .,
    scales = "free_y",
    space = "free_y",
    labeller = labeller(origin = c("GL" = "Greenland", "FO" = "Faroe Islands"))
  ) +

  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(min(northatlantic_ft$date), NA)) +

  theme_nordatlantisk_basis() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#777777", linewidth = 0.05),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
  )
```

## Political Parties {.unnumbered .unlisted}

Since 2004, MPs from the Faroe Islands were members of `r n2w(sum(political_parties$origin == "FO"))` different political parties. Voters in Greenland elected politicians from `r n2w(sum(political_parties$origin == "GL") - 2)` different political parties. However, two of the Greenlandic representatives -- Aleqa Hammond and Aki-Matilda Høegh-Dam -- switched party affiliation during their time as member of Folketinget and joined two relatively young parties (Nunatta Qitornai and Naleraq[^3]).

[^3]: Both parties have been formed rather recently -- Naleraq in 2014 [@krebsHerErPartii2014] and Nunatta Qitornai in 2017/2018 [@fieveNytPartiTaettere2018]. The latter has de facto been dissolved after the 2021 Inatsisartut election [@vestergaardhviidVittusQujaukitsoqMelder2025]. See @ahlnessNunattaQitornaiParty2020 for general information on Nunatta Qitornai and their policies.

The Northatlantic MPs usually are members of the two biggest political parties of Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands [@elklitElectoralSystemFair2020]. These parties then act as de-facto ethnic regional parties in Folketinget [@ackrenExploringRoleRegional2019]. Before political parties were established in Greenland in the 1970s [@billeGronlandskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025; @michelsenGronlandPartisystemUdvikling1979], MPs were elected independently. Since then, one of the two Greenlandic seats has been held by social democratic *Siumut* (SIU) for most of the time. Only recently has Siumut not been represented in Folketinget, due to the MPs in question switching party affiliations (see @fig-party-timeline). The 'second' Greenlandic seat was affiliated with centre-right *Atassut* (A) from 1977 to 2001. Since then, these MPs have been members of socialist *Inuit Ataqatigiit* (IA). This dominance by two political parties is in contrast to the Faroese situation, where the four biggest parties take turns more often [@billeFaeroskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025].

All represented political parties are listed in the [Appendix](#list-of-parties) with additional information (where available) on their positions from the ParlGov dataset [@doringParlGov2024Release2024]. @fig-party-timeline shows the allocation of Folketinget seats to political parties from Greenland and the Faroe Islands on a timeline. At no point in time were both MPs of Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands members of the same party. In the time frame covered by this dataset, the Faroe Islands have been represented by one left-wing and one right-wing political party in Folketinget except for one election period (2015--2019), as opposed to the Greenlandic MPs having belonged to two left-wing parties.

The Northatlantic MPs have sometimes been members of Danish parliamentary groups. Over the years, this has varied between no membership, informal association to full memberships [@harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, 17-18]. From 2001 until 2011, three Northatlantic MPs formed a separate parliamentary group ['Den Nordatlantiske Gruppe i Folketinget', @gadGronlandskeFolketingsmedlemmer2022; @harderFaeroskeOgGronlandske2022, S6].

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-party-timeline
#| fig-cap: Timeline of political parties from Greenland and the Faroe Islands with an MP in Folketinget since 2004. Dashed lines indicate election dates.

# collapse MP_dates timeline into non-overlapping party intervals
party_periods <- MP_dates %>%
  select(party, origin, start, end) %>%
  arrange(party, origin, start, end) %>%
  group_by(party, origin)

# join colours from political_parties
party_periods <- party_periods %>%
  left_join(political_parties %>% select("party", "full_name", "colour"), by = "party")

# sort parties with start date
party_periods <- party_periods %>%
  group_by(origin) %>%
  mutate(party = factor(party, levels = rev(unique(party[order(start)])))) %>%
  ungroup()

# set party name labels including UF
y_labels <- setNames(party_periods$full_name, party_periods$party)
y_labels <- c(y_labels, "UF" = "No Party Affiliation")

# set UF colour to grey
party_periods$colour[party_periods$party == "UF"] <- "#777777"

ggplot(party_periods, aes(x = start, xend = end, y = party, yend = party, color = colour)) +
  geom_segment(linewidth = 8, lineend = "butt") +
  scale_color_identity() +

  scale_y_discrete(labels = y_labels) +
  
  # add Folketing Election dates
  geom_vline(data = elections_ft, aes(xintercept = as.Date(date), linetype = election_type),
             color = "#000000", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Folketing Election" = "longdash"), name = "") +
  
  facet_grid(origin ~ ., scales = "free_y", space = "free_y",
             labeller = labeller(origin = c("FO" = "Faroe Islands", "GL" = "Greenland"))) +
  
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(min(northatlantic_ft$date), NA)) +
  
  theme_nordatlantisk_basis() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#777777", linewidth = 0.05),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank()
  )
```

## Voting Records {.unnumbered .unlisted}

The observations available in the dataset contain voting decisions by the four MPs representing Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands at the time of each roll call vote. The final dataset used in this analysis comprises 22 variables that are explained in detail in the [codebook](https://mtwente.github.io/nordatlantisk-ft/docs/codebook.html). It contains three main categories of information for each observation: There is information on each recorded vote by an MP including the actual type of vote cast as well as metadata on the origin (`GL`/`FO`) and the party affiliation of the politician in question. Then there is metadata on the roll call vote such as the overall voting result and the topic of each proposal including the responsible ministry. And finally, the dataset also contains variables that provide information on the cabinets in Denmark and Greenland resp. the Faroe Islands at the time of the observation, e.g. whether the MP's party is part of the cabinet or not.

```{r bad-roll-calls}
#| echo: false
#| message: false

# Count how many times each ballot_id appears
counts <- table(northatlantic_ft$roll_call_id)

# Find roll_call_id values that do NOT appear exactly 4 times
counts_df <- as.data.frame(counts)
bad_roll_call_id <- as.data.frame(names(counts[counts != 4]))

# calculate share of total observations
error_share <- (nrow(bad_roll_call_id) + sum(!roll_call_results_ft$roll_call_id %in% northatlantic_ft$roll_call_id))/nrow(northatlantic_ft)
```

There are a few observations where data on Folketinget's Open Data Platform is unavailable or incomplete: For `r sum(!roll_call_results_ft$roll_call_id %in% northatlantic_ft$roll_call_id)` roll call votes, there are no individual voting records available at all. And for `r n2w(nrow(bad_roll_call_id))` roll call votes, there are only three registered observations for Northatlantic MPs instead of four[^missing]. In total, these errors correspond to `r scales::percent(error_share, accuracy = 0.01)` of all data.

[^missing]: This might be due to a missing functionality on Folketinget's Open Data Platform, where it is not possible to query (former) members based on their constituency. Maybe I missed a short-term temporary replacement MP. However, since I was not able to find any hint about MPs that are not yet part of the dataset in other sources, this maybe really just is a database error.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-n-rollcall
#| fig-cap: Number of roll call votes per year (excluding 2004 and 2026 due to incomplete coverage in the dataset).

##| fig-height: 1.2

rollcalls_per_year <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  mutate(year = lubridate::year(date)) %>%
  filter(year != 2026) %>% # filtering out 2026 because it will distort
  filter(year != 2004) %>% # filtering also 2004 because records only start in October
  group_by(year) %>%
  summarise(
    n_rollcalls = n_distinct(roll_call_id),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

# compute global maximum for y-axis
y_max <- max(rollcalls_per_year$n_rollcalls, na.rm = TRUE) + 1 


ggplot(
  rollcalls_per_year,
  aes(x = factor(year), y = n_rollcalls)
) +
  
  geom_col(width = 0.7, fill = "#6195CF") +
  
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, y_max),
    breaks = c(seq(0, 600, 200), 700),
    labels = c(seq(0, 600, 200), 700),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.01))
  ) +
  
  theme_nordatlantisk_basis() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1),
    axis.ticks.x = element_blank(),
    axis.line.y.left = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#777777", linewidth = 0.05)
  )
```

```{r voting-blocks}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
# calculate share of roll call votes per block
blocks <- as.data.frame(table(northatlantic_ft$gvt_bloc_dk))
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-vote-types
#| tbl-cap: "Types of roll call votes."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

roll_call_summary <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  filter(roll_call_type_id %in% c(1, 2, 3, 4)) %>%
  count(roll_call_type_id, name = "n") %>%
  mutate(
    Type = case_when(
      roll_call_type_id == 1 ~ "Final Adoption",
      roll_call_type_id == 2 ~ "Committee Recommendation",
      roll_call_type_id == 3 ~ "Proposed Adoption",
      roll_call_type_id == 4 ~ "Proposed Amendment"
    )
  ) %>%
  select(ID = roll_call_type_id, Type, n)

kable(
  roll_call_summary,
  col.names = c("ID", "Type", "Count"),
  booktabs = TRUE,
  format = "latex"
)
```

During the timeframe covered by this dataset, there are `r floor(mean(rollcalls_per_year$n_rollcalls))` roll call votes in Folketinget per year on average, with a maximum number of `r max(rollcalls_per_year$n_rollcalls)` votes in `r rollcalls_per_year %>% slice_max(n_rollcalls, n = 1) %>% pull(year)` (@fig-n-rollcall). The dataset covers all types of roll call votes in Folketinget (@tbl-vote-types): `r scales::percent(length(northatlantic_ft$roll_call_type_id[northatlantic_ft$roll_call_type_id == "1"])/nrow(northatlantic_ft), accuracy = 0.1)` of the votes are final decisions on a proposal, and `r scales::percent(length(northatlantic_ft$roll_call_type_id[northatlantic_ft$roll_call_type_id == "4"])/nrow(northatlantic_ft), accuracy = 0.1)` are votes on amendments to a proposal. Overall, `r scales::percent(mean(northatlantic_ft$roll_call_pass, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.1)` of the proposals pass with a positive voting result.

The dataset spans across across six full cycles of Folketinget elections (and the last few months of the 2001--2005 election cycle). Within this timeframe, there have been seven elections to Inatsisartut in Greenland and five elections to the Faroese Løgting. Of the roll call votes covered in the dataset, `r scales::percent(blocks$Freq[blocks$Var1 == "left"]/sum(blocks$Freq), accuracy = 0.1)` took place during a cabinet formed by the red/left block was in office in Denmark (during blue/right block coalitions: `r scales::percent(blocks$Freq[blocks$Var1 == "right"]/sum(blocks$Freq), accuracy = 0.1)`, and for the current cross-block coalition: `r scales::percent(blocks$Freq[blocks$Var1 == "across"]/sum(blocks$Freq), accuracy = 0.1)`). The ministry responsible for each proposal being voted on is also a variable in the dataset. The most records refer to the Ministry of Finance, the Ministry of Justice, and the Ministry of Employment (@tbl-top-ministries). This has to be read with a grain of salt, since there are a lot of `NA` values and because designations[^full] change frequently so that e.g. 'Klima- og Energiministeriet' and 'Klima-, Energie- og Bygningsministeriet' etc. are counted as different entities. 

[^full]: Refer to the codebook for a [full list](https://mtwente.github.io/nordatlantisk-ft/docs/codebook.html#northatlantic_ftministry) of all `r n_distinct(northatlantic_ft$ministry, na.rm = TRUE)` designations that appear in the dataset.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-top-ministries
#| tbl-cap: "Most frequent values for `ministry`."
#| tbl-cap-location: bottom

northatlantic_ft %>%
  count(ministry, sort = TRUE) %>%
  slice_head(n = 5) %>%
  knitr::kable(
    col.names = c("Ministry", "n"),
    align = c("l", "r"),
    booktabs = TRUE,
    format = "latex"
  )
```

MPs can either vote for, against or neither for nor against a proposal. Additionally, absences are recorded. Looking at the North Atlantic MPs' voting records, it is striking how few times they actually cast a vote: Filtering for those cases results in `r length(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id[northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id != "3"])` non-absent observations (out of `r nrow(northatlantic_ft)` cases), translating to `r mean(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id == "3") %>% scales::percent(accuracy = 0.1)` of observations being coded as 'absent' (@fig-absence-share) -- an observation that corresponds well to the findings of previous research. The share of non-absent records is still low when compared to Folketinget voting behavior as a whole (@fig-ft-vote-distribution). Of the non-absent records, `r scales::percent(sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id == 1, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id != 3, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.1)` are votes in favor, `r scales::percent(sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id == 2, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id != 3, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.01)` are votes against, and `r scales::percent(sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id == 4, na.rm = TRUE) / sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id != 3, na.rm = TRUE), accuracy = 0.01)` are votes neither for nor against.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| fig-height: 1.2
#| label: fig-absence-share
#| fig-cap: Northatlantic MPs are listed as absent in 98% of the observations in this dataset.

# #| fig-env: "figure*" removed temporarily

# Compute proportions of vote types
vote_props <- northatlantic_ft %>%
  count(vote_type_id) %>%
  mutate(
    share = n / sum(n),
    vote_type = factor(vote_type_id,
                       levels = c(3, 4, 2, 1),
                       labels = c("absent", "abstention", "against", "for"))
  )

# Single horizontal bar plot
ggplot(vote_props, aes(x = 1, y = share, fill = vote_type)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.5) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(
    name = "Vote",
    labels = c("for", "against", "abstention", "absent"),
    values = c("#6195CF", "#F7CB45", "#777777", "#D1BBD7"),
    breaks = c("for", "against", "abstention", "absent")
  ) +

  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(),
    breaks = c(0, 0.05, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .015))
  ) +
  
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_nordatlantisk_basis() +
  theme(
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.y = element_blank(),
    axis.ticks.x = element_line(color = "#000000", linewidth = 0.1),
    panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(),
    legend.position = "top"
  )
```

It is self-evident that the MPs with the most observations in the dataset are those who are/were the longest-sitting members (@fig-votes-per-mp) -- Sjúrður Skaale (FO/C, `r sum(northatlantic_ft$MP_id == 262, na.rm = TRUE)` records), Edmund Joensen (FO/B, `r sum(northatlantic_ft$MP_id == 247, na.rm = TRUE)` records) and Aaja Chemnitz (GL/IA, `r sum(northatlantic_ft$MP_id == 15757, na.rm = TRUE)` records). As MPs are absent for most roll calls, @fig-votes-per-mp-filtered shows the distribution only with votes that were actually cast. Long-term membership, however, does not necessarily correspond with a larger number in registered votes, as demonstrated by Sjúrður Skaale's share of `r scales::percent(sum(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id[northatlantic_ft$MP_id == 262] != 3) / length(northatlantic_ft$vote_type_id[northatlantic_ft$MP_id == 262]), accuracy = 0.01)` non-absent records.

```{r, fig.pos = 'H'}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: fig-votes-per-mp
#| fig-cap: Full records coded by the type of vote cast (for, against, abstaining, absent).

plot_votes <- ggplot(northatlantic_ft_ordered, aes(y = plotting_name, fill = vote_type_id)) +
  geom_bar() +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, .05))) +
  scale_y_discrete() +
```

# Results

The results of the analysis are presented separately for each hypothesis followed by a broader assessment of the data and research design.

## H~1~: Participation Before/After 2009 {.unnumbered .unlisted}

<!-- * H~1~: *Participation in roll call voting increases after the Northatlantic Group is dissolved after the 2011 general election.* -->

I tested whether the participation rates changed as a result of changes in formalised cooperation between MPs in form of the Northatlantic Parliamentary Group -- regarding the official ending of the group in 2011 as cut-off date as well as the de-facto ending of inner-constituency cooperation between Greenlandic MPs in this formalised setting.

The Faroese MPs show no difference in participation rates with neither 2009 nor 2011 set as break points. With the Farose MPs considered as control group without group-based cooperation incentives, this was to be expected. However, no effect is detected for the Greenlandic MPs either, with the difference-in-differences model showing no relevant changes in participation rates when taking the end of group cooperation as 'treatment' (@tbl-did).

A visual inspection of @fig-vote-share-per-year supports this finding. The level of participation in roll call votes (i.e. casting a vote either for, against, or neither for nor against) generally varies over time. In general, rather low proportions of non-absent votes -- rarely exceeding 3% -- are most common in the dataset. However, the share of votes cast among MPs from the Faroe Islands increased in recent years (2023 and 2025, but not 2024). This observation is not true for the Greenlandic MPs, where a single peak is recorded in the data for 2015. The latter can be attributed to (then) newly elected MP Aaja Chemnitz (IA/GL) while the majority of the votes recorded from Faroese MPs since 2023, a remarkable increase in share of non-absent records, were cast by MP Anna Falkenberg (B/FO) who was elected to Folketinget at the end of 2022.

Overall, there is no evidence to support the hypothesis that cooperation within the Northatlantic Parliamentary group had any influence on the level of voting activity of the Northatlantic MPs during the timeframe covered by this dataset.

::: {#fig-vote-share-per-year}
<!-- in a fenced div because of the dynamically updating caption -->

## H~2~: Bloc Cohesion {.unnumbered .unlisted}

<!-- * H~2~: *Voting cohesion among MPs from the same constituency is higher than voting cohesion among MPs from the same political bloc.* -->

```{r setup-krippendorff}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

krippendorf_result <- as.data.frame(t(unlist(kripp.alpha(vote_matrix_t, method = "nominal"))))

alpha_table <- data.frame(
  Alpha = round(as.numeric(krippendorf_result$value), 3),
  Subjects = krippendorf_result$subjects,
  Raters = krippendorf_result$raters
)
```

The presence of voting cohesion was tested with regard to differences between MP origin, bloc affiliation, and party stances on independence from Denmark. As prerequisite for cohesive voting behavior, the dataset was subset to include only those cases where more than one MPs participated, resulting in observations concerning `r sum(complete.cases(cohesion_df$cohesion))` roll calls. As a basic summary measure for agreement levels between political parties, I calculated Krippendorff's Alpha (@tbl-krippendorffs-alpha). The resulting $\alpha$ = `r round(as.numeric(krippendorf_result$value), 3)` indicates that the voting records indeed show a fairly high level of inter-voter agreement.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-krippendorffs-alpha
#| tbl-cap: "Krippendorff's $\\alpha$ for voter agreement"
#| tbl-cap-location: top
#| tbl-pos: "H"

kable(alpha_table, booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrr", format = "latex")
```

This first indicative result was then developed further by looking at pairwise agreements. I calculated pairwise agreement rates based on origin, political bloc association and on the position on independence (from Denmark) of the corresponding political party. Agreement rates do not differ substantially between pairs of MPs that were elected in the same constituency and pairs who were not (@tbl-pairwise-agreement-origin). Also, agreement rates are basically the same for pairs of MPs that belong to parties with the same position on independence from Denmark and for pairs of MPs who do not (@tbl-pairwise-agreement-independence). However, I find the highest level of pairwise agreement for MPs belonging to the same political bloc (@tbl-pairwise-agreement-bloc). This agreement rate also drops considerably for pairs of MPs from different blocs.

These results suggest that, within the context of this dataset, similar political positions, indicated by association with one of the two blocs, are a more relevant factor in explaining observed co-voting compared to representing the same constituency. In this sense, the results do not support H~2~. But because both Greenlandic MPs have belonged to the same political bloc during the whole timeframe covered by this dataset, cross-bloc agreement could only ever occur with involvement of at least one of the Faroese MPs anyway. This setup, in addition to the low number of roll calls with more than one recorded vote, limits the usefulness of agreement rates as indicators even further.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-pairwise-agreement-origin
#| tbl-cap: "Origin-Based Pairwise Agreement Rates"
#| tbl-cap-location: top

kable(
  origin_agreement_rate,
  col.names = c("Same Origin", "Agreement Rate", "n"),
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = "lrr",
  format = "latex"
)

## same_origin = TRUE => cohesion within Greenland / within Faroe Islands
## same_origin = FALSE => cross-origin agreement
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-pairwise-agreement-independence
#| tbl-cap: "Pairwise Agreement Rates based on Parties' Positions on Independence"
#| tbl-cap-location: top

kable(
  independence_agreement_rate,
  col.names = c("Same Independ. Stance", "Agreement Rate", "n"),
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = "lrr",
  format = "latex"
)

## same_independence_stance = TRUE => cohesion across parties with the same stance on independence
## same_independence_stance = FALSE => cohesion across parties with different stances on independence
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-pairwise-agreement-bloc
#| tbl-cap: "Bloc-Based Pairwise Agreement Rates"
#| tbl-cap-location: top

kable(
  bloc_agreement_rate,
  col.names = c("Same Bloc", "Agreement Rate", "n"),
  booktabs = TRUE,
  align = "lrr",
  format = "latex"
)

## same_bloc = TRUE => cohesion within parties from the same bloc
## same_bloc = FALSE => cohesion within parties across different blocs
```

## H~3~: Pivotality {.unnumbered .unlisted}

<!-- * H~3~: *The closer the parliamentary balance between government and opposition, the more often Northatlantic MPs participate in roll call votes* -->

Next, I tested the relation between voting participation and the parliamentary seat share distributon between party blocks using two different models (@tbl-pivotality-model). With the first model, I addressed the question of whether MPs participate more in votes with a close outcome, assuming that in most cases, close results can be anticipated. The results showed that there is no evidence to support the hypothesis based on this model (Model 1a).

Model 2a on the relation between the number of cabinet parties' seats in parliament and participation rates among Northatlantic MPs indicates a negative effect: As the number of parliamentary seats of cabinet parties increases, participation of Northatlantic MPs decreases. This is exactly as expected: When governing parties can rely on more votes from members of their own parties, there is less need for including Northatlantic MPs in building of parliamentary majorities.

Model 1b and 2b, including the type of coalition, indicate that participation of Northatlantic MPs is higher in cross-bloc coalitions. This is also in line with my expectations. However, since there has only been one cross-bloc cabinet in the dataset, this is not really a generalisation to make. Additionally, the higher level of participation during this cabinet appears to be almost entirely the result of the voting behavior of Anna Falkenberg (B/FO), judging by a visual inspection of @fig-vote-share-per-year and @fig-votes-per-mp-filtered. Still, it could be interesting to compare participation patterns under other cross-bloc cabinets, e.g. the Anker Jørgensen III cabinet (1978--1979, Socialdemokratiet/Venstre).

# Appendix {.appendix}

## List of MPs {.appendix .unnumbered .unlisted}

Since Folketinget's Open Data Platform does not provide a function to search for (former) MPs per constituency, this list was compiled based on previous work [e.g. @harderSupplerendeMaterialeFaeroske2022; @gadGronlandskeFolketingsmedlemmer2022; @billeFaeroskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025; @billeGronlandskeFolketingsmedlemmer2025] and newspaper reports, as well as by searching for strings like 'grønland\*' and 'færøsk\*' on the Open Data Platform. This is not a very efficient way of searching since it will also return all MPs who at one point were members of Folketinget's commissions on Greenland or the Faroe Islands, or, additionally, all MPs who mention one of these places in their (free text) biography (this concerns e.g. former workplaces etc.). If there should be any MP still missing from this list, it is however easy to add them to the dataset and to reproduce the workflow.

The nordatlantisk-ft repository also contains complementary metadata on the MPs in this dataset, amongst other things a [complete membership timeline](https://github.com/mtwente/nordatlantisk-ft/blob/21774728bf1cd50901ba2b2fe0341018cc9c6ac9/data/processed/csv/MP_dates.csv) including temporary replacements, and a data frame [linking](https://github.com/mtwente/nordatlantisk-ft/blob/21774728bf1cd50901ba2b2fe0341018cc9c6ac9/data/processed/csv/MP_names.csv) each MP to the corresponding Wikidata item from where further information can be inferred.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| label: tbl-MPs
#| tbl-colwidths: [12, 30, 25, 10, 10, 13]

MPs <- mp_names %>%
  select(-wikidata_id) %>%
  select(origin, everything()) %>%
  arrange(origin, surname)

printable_names <- c("Origin", "Surname(s)", "First Name(s)", "MP ID", "Party", "Substitute")

kable(MPs, caption = "List of MPs from Greenland and the Faroe Islands in Folketinget (October 2004 -- January 2026).", col.names = printable_names)
```

## List of Parties {.appendix .unnumbered .unlisted}

@tbl-blocs and @tbl-party-parlgov provide information on the political parties that make up the *nordatlantisk-ft* dataset. The categorisation of the parties with regard to the political bloc they are affiliated to and their stance on independence is based on @ackrenPoliticalPartiesGreenland2015, @ahlnessNunattaQitornaiParty2020 [167], and @westMPFirefightingWhen2018 [103].

Data on the association with a party family and on the party positions in @tbl-party-parlgov are taken from the 2024 ParlGov release [@doringParlGov2024Release2024]. ParlGov does, however, not include metadata on the two Greenlandic parties that have been represented in Folketinget only recently -- Nunatta Qitornai in 2018/2019 and, since 2025, Naleraq. Additionally, Aleqa Hammond was MP without party affiliation from `r format(MP_dates$start[MP_dates$period_id == "hammond_2"], "%B %d, %Y")` to `r format(MP_dates$end[MP_dates$period_id == "hammond_2"], "%B %d, %Y")` [@twenteNordatlantiskft2026].

```{r}
    left_right, state_market,
    liberty_authority, anti_pro_eu
  )
```

### Overall Voting Patterns {.appendix .unnumbered .unlisted}

@fig-ft-vote-distribution shows the distribution of vote types per roll call vote for all MPs in Folketinget. At first glance, it stands out how the number of absent MPs hovers around 70 for all years covered by the timeline. This is due to Folketinget being a 'working parliament', where MPs are regularly cleared from taking part in the plenary sessions which are "mostly poorly attended" [@arterNordicParliamentsMuchofamuchness2016, 214].

```{r, fig.pos = 'H'}
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| label: fig-ft-vote-distribution
#| fig-cap: Density plot visualising the number of votes cast by all MPs for each roll call vote by type.

make_density_plot <- function(data, y_var, title, low_col, high_col) {
  
  ggplot(data, aes(x = date, y = {{ y_var }})) +
    
    geom_bin2d(aes(fill = after_stat(count)), bins = 80) +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = low_col, high = high_col) +
    
    scale_x_date(
      breaks = as.Date(c("2005-01-01", "2015-01-01", "2025-01-01")),
      date_labels = "%Y",
      expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, .05))
    ) +
    
    scale_y_continuous(
      limits = c(0, 179),
      labels = c(0, 50, 100, 150, 179),
      breaks = c(0, 50, 100, 150, 179)
    ) +
    
    ggtitle(title) +
    
    theme_nordatlantisk_basis() +
    theme(
      axis.title.y = element_blank(),
      axis.line.y.left = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "none",
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#777777", linewidth = 0.05),
      plot.title = element_text(size = 8),
      axis.text.x = element_text(size = rel(0.7))
    )
}

scatterplot_for <- make_density_plot(northatlantic_ft, ft_for, "for", "#6195CF", "#436890")

scatterplot_against <- make_density_plot(northatlantic_ft, ft_against, "against", "#F7CB45", "#ac8e30")

scatterplot_abstention <- make_density_plot(northatlantic_ft, ft_abstention, "abstention", "#777777", "#535353")

scatterplot_absent <- make_density_plot(northatlantic_ft, ft_absent, "absent", "#D1BBD7", "#928296")

patchworked_plot <- scatterplot_for + scatterplot_against + scatterplot_abstention + scatterplot_absent + plot_layout(ncol = 4, axes = "collect")

patchworked_plot
```
